articles.title_zh: Azerbaijan Resumes Fig Imports from China
articles.content_orig:
In January–August 2026, Azerbaijan imported 53 tonnes of fresh and dried figs worth a total of $246,000. Compared with the same period last year, import volumes increased by 8%, while the value of imports declined by 6%, reports EastFruit , citing ABC.az .
Saudi Arabia and Turkey were the main suppliers of figs to the Azerbaijani market. During the eight-month period, Azerbaijan imported 22.5 tonnes of figs worth $52,300 from Saudi Arabia, compared with no supplies from this country a year earlier. Turkey supplied 19.3 tonnes worth $134,400, increasing its export volume by 51% and value by 54%.
Rad also: Seasonal Fruit Prices Rise in Azerbaijan: Sellers Blame Higher Logistics Costs
In addition, Azerbaijan imported 6 tonnes of figs worth $28,400 from China, 3.5 tonnes worth $21,300 from Iran, and 1.6 tonnes worth $8,800 from Uzbekistan. Uzbekistan, meanwhile, sharply reduced its supplies, by 95% in volume and 94.3% in value.
Chinese supplies were a particularly notable change in the import structure. Azerbaijan resumed fig imports from China after a break of one year and 11 months.

articles.title_orig: Ex-military chief Gadi Eisenkot, opponent of Netanyahu, tapped to form government
articles.title_zh: Ex-military chief Gadi Eisenkot, opponent of Netanyahu, tapped to form government
articles.content_orig:
In a setback to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu , his main rival will be tasked with forming the next Israeli government, placing him one step closer to ousting Israel’s longest-serving leader, even as the path remains complicated.
Gadi Eisenkot , a retired military chief who led the centrist Yashar party in the October 27 election, will have up to six weeks to try and assemble a coalition to replace Netanyahu. But his path to power is fraught with political obstacles and divisions within the opposition itself.
President Isaac Herzog will officially give Eisenkot the mandate to form a government on Sunday, his office said in a statement. Herzog’s decision followed two days of consultations last week with all parties elected to the Knesset.
Eisenkot secured the support of 67 members of the incoming Knesset, including 19 from the two Arab parties. Netanyahu received just 46 recommendations. A notable crack in his once-loyal bloc was exposed during the consultations when United Torah Judaism, a traditional Netanyahu ally, declined to recommend him.
Yet Herzog’s decision does not automatically remove Netanyahu from power. Eisenkot has a mandate and a parliamentary majority on paper, but not yet a governing coalition.
Eisenkot is pushing to form what he calls a “national emergency government” and to swear in a minority government as soon as possible. It would comprise the four Jewish opposition parties, which together hold 48 seats: his own Yashar; Together, led by former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid; Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu, and the left-wing Democrats, led by Yair Golan.
He has set four conditions for joining: recognizing Israel as a Jewish, democratic, liberal, and egalitarian state, commitment to the values of the Declaration of Independence, universal service – whether military, national, or civilian – and recognition of Hamas as a terrorist organization.
The last condition effectively rules out the Arab parties from sitting in the Cabinet. But they could still support the government from outside, providing a parliamentary safety net. Israeli law requires only a simple majority to establish a government. Removing one is far more difficult, requires an absolute majority of 61 votes who support an alternative government. (The Knesset has 120 seats.)
Eisenkot’s central obstacle is Avigdor Liberman. The Yisrael Beitenu leader and, at different times, former defense, foreign affairs and finance minister, has ruled out any government dependent on the Arab parties. A minority government, he argues, will be short-lived, and in the long run, will only strengthen Netanyahu. “We’ll have Netanyahu come back with 70 seats for another four years, and from there it’s a short road to annihilation,” Liberman wrote on X on Friday.
Instead, Liberman proposed a different route. Dropping his years-long veto on the ultra-Orthodox parties, he urged to make a “maximum effort” to form a coalition of 61 lawmakers with the two ultra-Orthodox parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism, and without the Joint List and Ra’am. Once it is formed, he added, three or four lawmakers from the Likud may defect.
Trump’s Election Day bombshell on Israel points to historic shift in US politics
That plan, however, clashes with one of the opposition’s core commitments: to end the blanket draft exemption for ultra-Orthodox men from mandatory military service. The ultra-Orthodox parties are pressing for legislation that would enshrine the exemption, and Eisenkot, Liberman and the rest of the opposition pledged universal service throughout the campaign. Moreover, one of the ultra-Orthodox parties remains loyal to Netanyahu.
Netanyahu, who lost his parliamentary majority, is also applying heavy pressure against any Jewish-Arab political cooperation. He is challenging the election results and claims the vote was “stolen” by Arab parties by bribery and foreign funding. David Zini, his loyalist Shin Bet director, has been pushing to investigate Arab politicians without any public evidence.
In a video statement Saturday, Netanyahu warned that if a minority government is formed with the Arab parties’ support, Israel will “simply not survive.” Instead, he called for a national unity government with his entire bloc, which includes far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties. Netanyahu called for “all Zionist parties that want to preserve our one and only state of the Jewish people.”
Eisenkot dismissed his message as a “pathetic spin.” In a statement, the Yashar party said, “If the Likud wants a broad unity government, it is more than welcome to announce the dissolution of the alliance with the extremists and enter a government under Prime Minister Eisenkot.”
Eisenkot’s first test comes Tuesday with the swearing in of the new Knesset. The opposition intends to replace Netanyahu’s Knesset speaker, weakening his grip on power and allowing the opposition parties to begin taking some actions, such as forming a state commission of inquiry into the security failures that led to the October 7, 2023, attack by Hamas. Starting Sunday, Eisenkot will have 28 days to negotiate with other parties over Cabinet posts, budgets and policies, with a possible 14-day extension. If he fails, the mandate passes to Netanyahu for another four weeks.
Eisenkot said on Friday he intends to form a government as quickly as possible, framing the moment as a national emergency. “A situation in which a caretaker prime minister in the minority, who has lost the trust of the people in such an extreme way, continues to operate the security system and law enforcement authorities, is a dangerous situation that must not continue even for one more day,” he wrote on X.

articles.title_orig: Crypto industry braces for reckoning over Trump ties
articles.title_zh: Crypto industry braces for reckoning over Trump ties
articles.content_orig:
This article was contributed by Binance
The second Trump term has put cryptocurrencies on center stage, not only as a policy priority but as a source of real income for the president himself.
The country is suddenly talking about Bitcoin reserves, government-backed stockpiles and Trump’s crypto businesses generating more revenue than his real estate empire. The market is responding in ways not seen before. As of September 25, 2026, the Bitcoin to USD rate was $83,376.06, according to data from Binance. And Washington might have as much influence over the price as basic supply and demand.
In March 2025, Trump signed an executive order creating a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve. This pool was initially filled with Bitcoin already in government hands, seized during various criminal and civil forfeiture cases, according to an official statement from the White House. Alongside that, there’s a Digital Asset Stockpile for other coins. The plan is simple enough: Hold Bitcoin like the U.S. holds gold or oil, and make it a national reserve asset.
More than a year later, this reserve is still mostly for show. The administration keeps insisting that Congress needs to step in before things take off, and while a bill is expected to be reintroduced under a fresh name, so far it’s all been talk, according to Yahoo Finance. Early numbers suggested the government had about 200,000 BTC, though the U.S. Marshals Service isn’t so sure about that, according to CCN.
That Bitcoin reserve was just the warm-up. In July 2025, Trump greenlit the GENIUS Act, the first real federal framework for stablecoins backed by U.S. dollars. Now, payment stablecoins get official recognition: They’re neither securities nor commodities, finally cutting through years of confusion, according to a fact sheet from the White House.
Banks, asset managers and large corporations have shown renewed interest in stablecoins following the regulatory clarity. Regulated stablecoins are becoming a preferred tool for settling tokenized securities and on-chain payments, a shift that could open the door to significant new capital, according to Yahoo Finance and Investing.com. The Trump administration has also appointed crypto-friendly regulators across federal agencies. In May 2026, Trump signed another executive order requiring regulators to drop rules that kept banks from partnering with fintech and crypto companies, according to a fact sheet from the White House .
All these regulatory resets have supercharged the industry and Trump’s business interests. His 2025 financial disclosure, sent to the Office of Government Ethics and made public on June 30, 2026, shows digital assets as his top income stream. His companies pulled in nearly $800 million from World Liberty Financial, the crypto project he co-founded with his sons. That includes $520 million from token sales, and another $250 million by selling stakes in the venture. On top of that, Trump scored another $635 million through sales of the $TRUMP meme coin, which he launched just before returning to office. All this has been reported by Time and Reuters.
Sum it up, and Trump’s family crypto businesses brought in more than $1.4 billion in reported income for 2025. Reuters says crypto was the single biggest driver of his $2.2 billion in total disclosed earnings, beating out real estate and legal settlements combined. When he was called out for it, Trump told reporters, “You know why I’m profiting, because the stock market’s going up, everybody’s profiting,” according to Reuters. For context, his crypto income from the same venture in 2024 was about $57 million, so it grew more than tenfold in just one year, riding the wave of policy changes, according to BBC.
It’s not just empty promises. Companies in the sector have started making real moves thanks to regulatory clarity. Stablecoin issuers, payment platforms and crypto on/off ramp providers are citing the GENIUS Act as the reason they’re ramping up U.S. operations instead of dodging them, according to The Economic Times.
Banks that used to steer clear of crypto because of a 2022 FDIC directive can now roll out digital asset products that follow the rules, according to Legal500.
Dollar moves matter to Bitcoin buyers. The Press Banner’s money column on protecting your portfolio from a falling dollar covers the same concern that has drawn some investors toward Bitcoin during Trump’s second term.
Has the U.S. government bought more Bitcoin for its reserve?
No, not yet. The Strategic Bitcoin Reserve, created in March 2025, only includes Bitcoin seized through criminal and civil cases.
Does the GENIUS Act regulate Bitcoin itself?
No. The GENIUS Act is purely about U.S. dollar-backed stablecoins. It forces issuers to back their tokens one-to-one with cash and Treasury securities, and to publish monthly reserve reports.
How much has Bitcoin moved in September 2026 alone?
It ran from about $76,800 on September 2 to $83,376.06 on September 25, 2026, according to Binance.

articles.title_orig: Earthquake hits central Japan, injuring more than 20 people
articles.title_zh: Earthquake hits central Japan, injuring more than 20 people
articles.content_orig:
More than 20 people have been injured after a strong earthquake shook central Japan, shattering store windows and sending people fleeing buildings, according to local media and authorities.
The magnitude 5.7 quake struck at 1:04am local time on Sunday (16:00 GMT Saturday) at a depth of about 40km (25 miles) in western Shizuoka Prefecture, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency.
More than 20 people were injured in the Aichi and Shizuoka prefectures, the Kyodo news agency cited authorities as saying.
A wide area near Aichi Prefecture was affected, including the city of Hamamatsu, the ancient capitals of Kyoto and Nara, and the prefectures of Yamanashi, where Mount Fuji is located, and Gifu.
No tsunami warning was issued, Kyodo reported.
The quake was not felt in Tokyo, which is far from the epicentre.
Japanese television showed shattered shop windows and shards of glass scattered across streets. A bookstore was left with mounds of books that had fallen from the shelves.
Some of the injured had fallen on the stairs as they tried to flee, the Associated Press news agency reported.
The meteorological agency warned people to be ready for possible strong quakes in the coming week, especially the next two to three days.
“Please be on the lookout for mudslides, falling rocks and the possible effects from rainfall,” agency official Ayataka Ebita told reporters.
He said no apparent change had been detected so far in the Nankai Trough, an underwater ocean trench where two major tectonic plates meet under parts of Japan, where scientists say a megaquake could occur.
Some local train services were suspended, while the Shinkansen bullet trains were running at slower speeds in affected areas as a precautionary measure.
Trains on the Tokaido Shinkansen line, which connects Tokyo and Osaka, were delayed between Shizuoka and Gifu-Hashima stations after safety checks, rail operator JR Central said.

articles.title_orig: "Congress will investigate": Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang faces probe over alleged Chinese spy ties
articles.title_zh: "Congress will investigate": Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang faces probe over alleged Chinese spy ties
articles.content_orig:
Three House Republican committee leaders asked Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to sit for a closed-door briefing on his relationship with a tech executive reportedly identified as a Chinese intelligence asset.
"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's access to sensitive U.S. technology and information," the GOP lawmakers wrote in a letter to Huang unveiled Thursday, using the acronym for the People's Republic of China.
They are seeking information on Huang's interactions with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, as well as Nvidia's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage," they wrote in the brief message, which is dated Wednesday.
The letter does not specify which reports it is referring to. But The New York Times reported last week that U.S. intelligence found Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen determined to be funneling information to Beijing, had "developed a close relationship" with Jensen Huang.
President Donald Trump , who himself has forged close ties with Jensen Huang as he champions the U.S. artificial intelligence industry, was briefed about a year ago on those intelligence findings, the Times reported.
Trump "chose not to do anything with the information," according to the newspaper, which cited interviews with people briefed on the surveillance and other sources.
The letter to Huang was signed by House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., Select Committee on China Chairman John Moolenaar, R-Mich., and House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford, R-Ark.
Nvidia did not directly respond when asked by CNBC to comment on the letter and confirm whether Huang would attend the lawmakers' proposed briefing.
Nvidia instead provided a statement that largely mirrored the one it previously sent the Times, in which a spokesperson suggested Jensen Huang's interactions with Alice Huang were no different from his meetings with other executive clients.
"Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets—and zero information relevant to national security," the spokesperson said in the statement.
"Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year," the spokesperson said. "We're confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know."
A spokeswoman for Mast did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for additional information. Megaspeed did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment.
The lawmakers invited the Nvidia CEO to appear for an in-person joint briefing on Nov. 18. Nvidia is scheduled to report its third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17.
"China's access to that sensitive U.S. tech is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress," the committee leaders wrote. "It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk."

articles.title_orig: NASA unveils $10B Moon base contract as SpaceX, Blue Origin join lunar gold rush
articles.title_zh: NASA unveils $10B Moon base contract as SpaceX, Blue Origin join lunar gold rush
articles.content_orig:
NASA announced its new PROMISE rover will launch aboard a Blue Origin lander and reach the moon's south pole by late 2028.
NASA announced Saturday that Elon Musk's SpaceX, Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin and six other aerospace companies are eligible to compete for up to $10 billion in lunar delivery contracts as the agency advances plans to establish a permanent base on the moon.
The announcement, made at the MAX POWER aerospace expo and air show at Kennedy Space Center in Florida, expands NASA 's commercial lunar program, bringing together private companies to deliver scientific equipment, technology and infrastructure to the moon's south pole.
The new Commercial Lunar Payload Services framework has a maximum combined value of $10 billion over 10 years, with the figure representing a ceiling for future task orders, not money already awarded to participating companies.
VIRGIN GALACTIC UNVEILS NEW SPACESHIP APEIRON, TARGETS COMMERCIAL SPACEFLIGHT RETURN IN 2027
An animation depicts a rover traveling across the lunar surface. NASA announced plans on Saturday to develop a nuclear-powered rover for exploration near the moon's south pole. (NASA / Unknown)
Alongside SpaceX and Blue Origin, NASA selected Firefly Aerospace, Intuitive Machines, iSpace US, Lockheed Martin Space, Northrop Grumman Space Systems and Voyager Technologies to compete for future lunar delivery missions.
"We are building the Moon Base mission by mission," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in a statement.
"When our astronauts return to the Moon, they will arrive with the first elements of the Moon Base already waiting for them on the surface."
NASA also increased the maximum value of its existing CLPS contract from $2.6 billion to $4.2 billion to support the initial phase of its Moon base plans.
JEFF BEZOS REVEALS HIS VISION FOR AMERICA'S NEXT FRONTIER — FROM AI TO THE MOON
An artist's rendering shows NASA's planned Moon base near the lunar south pole. The agency announced new contracts on Saturday to support a sustained human presence on the Moon. (NASA / Unknown)
Beyond the new contracting framework, Blue Origin secured a separate $94 million base contract to deliver NASA's nuclear-powered PROMISE rover to the lunar South Pole, with an additional $140 million available through a performance-based option.
The six-wheeled rover, formally named the "Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping, and In-Situ Exploration," will examine the lunar surface and subsurface, including regions believed to harbor water ice that could help support a sustained human presence.
NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory will build the rover using spare flight components and engineering test models from its Curiosity and Perseverance Mars rovers, an approach the agency says will reduce development costs.
'DEFUND MUSK': FORMER CLINTON CABINET OFFICIAL URGES DEMOCRATS TO TARGET SPACEX FOUNDER
Blue Origin's Blue Moon Mark 1 (MK1) lunar surface lander. (NASA)
Blue Origin will use its Mark 1 lunar lander to deliver the rover, and NASA is targeting a late-2028 launch for an 18-month mission.
The agency also awarded six transportation task orders worth approximately $1.3 billion combined to Arrow Science and Technology, Blue Origin and Impulse Space.
Those missions will test technologies for moving cargo between Earth and the Moon, including navigation systems and robotic drones intended to scout potential landing areas.
NASA selected SpaceX for a separate demonstration under an existing lunar logistics contract to deploy communications satellites aboard its Starship rocket into the region between Earth and the Moon in 2028.
The demonstration is intended to help NASA develop communications networks connecting astronauts, mission controllers and future lunar infrastructure.
NASA also announced awards to Honeybee Robotics, a Blue Origin company, Redwire and Yank Technologies for components of a planned lunar power and communications tower.

The system will combine solar power and wireless power transfer to support operations on the Moon's surface.
NASA says the projects will help establish a sustained American presence on the Moon's South Pole, with commercial partners delivering equipment and infrastructure needed before astronauts arrive.
The agency ultimately hopes to use its lunar operations as a foundation for crewed missions to Mars one day.

articles.title_orig: Trump's Recent Warning Is Sending Shockwaves Through Wall Street. Here's What It Could Mean for Your Retirement Savings.
articles.title_zh: Trump's Recent Warning Is Sending Shockwaves Through Wall Street. Here's What It Could Mean for Your Retirement Savings.
articles.content_orig:
Love him or hate him, President Donald Trump's time in the White House has historically correlated with strong stock market returns. In fact, the benchmark S&P 500 ( ^GSPC +0.31% ) is up by over 39% since his inauguration in late 2024, showcasing widespread optimism among many on Wall Street.
So far, excitement about his pro-business policies has helped investors overlook severe macroeconomic challenges like tariffs, inflation, and unsustainable deficit spending. Let's dig deeper to see how much longer the honeymoon period might last and determine what effect the recent midterm results may have on market performance in the near term.
Like many Republican presidents, Trump has embraced a largely pro-business stance, passing the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which featured tax cuts and deregulation. The administration has also struck a favorable tone toward new energy projects and data center construction, which is especially important for the U.S. tech sector as it embarks on one of its largest infrastructure buildouts in history to support generative AI .
That said, it is increasingly clear that this one industry is helping prop up an otherwise lackluster stock market and (arguably) struggling economy.
According to CME Group, the information technology sector now accounts for a whopping 40% of the S&P 500's market cap. This level of concentration is risky in and of itself. But it is also allowing Wall Street to ignore the growing scale of macroeconomic challenges in the US.
Many of the biggest economic challenges stem from the administration's deliberate policies. These include Trump's tariffs, which have helped bring the average U.S. levy on all imports to around 9.6%, and the war in Iran, which has sent Brent crude prices up 55% since the start of the year.
US inflation now stands at 3.7%, well above the Federal Reserve's 2% target, forcing the central bank to keep rates elevated to control consumer prices. This has also corresponded with soaring Treasury bond yields as investors get nervous about the government's ability to manage its $40 trillion in debt.
Treasury bonds represent the risk-free rate in the economy. And when they rise, they can reduce investor appetite for risky growth stocks while also increasing the cost of capital these businesses need to expand. The Trump administration doesn't have a convincing strategy to fix these issues.
In an October interview with Time Magazine, Trump suggested that higher levels of inflation could help pay down the debt "very rapidly". The logic is that by devaluing U.S. currency, inflation will also devalue the national debt and make it easier to manage. These remarks should be taken as a warning that the administration may be willing to maintain its current inflationary fiscal policies over the coming years.
Image source: Getty Images.
Inflation is one of the most devastating things for investors and retirement savers because it constantly erodes both savings and financial market returns. Even if you earn the S&P 500's average annual return of 10%, an inflation rate of 3.7% takes your real rate of return to a much less impressive 6.3%. That said, this isn't the time to panic.
Over the long haul, the U.S. has shown a remarkable ability to self-correct and bounce back from crises, and this time probably won't be the exception. The recent midterm results could impose some checks and balances on the Iran war and on some of the government's most extreme spending plans (such as a proposed $1.5 trillion military budget), which could help calm the bond market and bring down inflation.
Yes, the U.S. economic situation remains uncertain, but there may be light at the end of the tunnel. Investors should also focus on diversifying their portfolios across a variety of asset classes to avoid being overly exposed to downside risk in any particular one.

A minority government, he argues, will be short-lived, and in the long run, will only strengthen Netanyahu. “We’ll have Netanyahu come back with 70 seats for another four years, and from there it’s a short road to annihilation,” Liberman wrote on X on Friday.
Instead, Liberman proposed a different route. Dropping his years-long veto on the ultra-Orthodox parties, he urged to make a “maximum effort” to form a coalition of 61 lawmakers with the two ultra-Orthodox parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism, and without the Joint List and Ra’am. Once it is formed, he added, three or four lawmakers from the Likud may defect.
Trump’s Election Day bombshell on Israel points to historic shift in US politics
That plan, however, clashes with one of the opposition’s core commitments: to end the blanket draft exemption for ultra-Orthodox men from mandatory military service. The ultra-Orthodox parties are pressing for legislation that would enshrine the exemption, and Eisenkot, Liberman and the rest of the opposition pledged universal service throughout the campaign. Moreover, one of the ultra-Orthodox parties remains loyal to Netanyahu.
Netanyahu, who lost his parliamentary majority, is also applying heavy pressure against any Jewish-Arab political cooperation. He is challenging the election results and claims the vote was “stolen” by Arab parties by bribery and foreign funding. David Zini, his loyalist Shin Bet director, has been pushing to investigate Arab politicians without any public evidence.
In a video statement Saturday, Netanyahu warned that if a minority government is formed with the Arab parties’ support, Israel will “simply not survive.” Instead, he called for a national unity government with his entire bloc, which includes far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties. Netanyahu called for “all Zionist parties that want to preserve our one and only state of the Jewish people.”
Eisenkot dismissed his message as a “pathetic spin.” In a statement, the Yashar party said, “If the Likud wants a broad unity government, it is more than welcome to announce the dissolution of the alliance with the extremists and enter a government under Prime Minister Eisenkot.”
Eisenkot’s first test comes Tuesday with the swearing in of the new Knesset. The opposition intends to replace Netanyahu’s Knesset speaker, weakening his grip on power and allowing the opposition parties to begin taking some actions, such as forming a state commission of inquiry into the security failures that led to the October 7, 2023, attack by Hamas. Starting Sunday, Eisenkot will have 28 days to negotiate with other parties over Cabinet posts, budgets and policies, with a possible 14-day extension. If he fails, the mandate passes to Netanyahu for another four weeks.
Eisenkot said on Friday he intends to form a government as quickly as possible, framing the moment as a national emergency. “A situation in which a caretaker prime minister in the minority, who has lost the trust of the people in such an extreme way, continues to operate the security system and law enforcement authorities, is a dangerous situation that must not continue even for one more day,” he wrote on X.

articles.title_orig: Who is Qiulae Wong, the outsider who could decide New Zealand's next government?
articles.title_zh: Who is Qiulae Wong, the outsider who could decide New Zealand's next government?
articles.content_orig:
New Zealand voters face weeks of political limbo after a knife-edge election left the country’s conservative coalition government at risk of losing its majority following just a single term in office.
Saturday’s preliminary results show Prime Minister Christopher Luxon’s National-led coalition with a paper-thin majority. But the margin is so tight, a small variance in the final tally could yet leave the opposition left-wing bloc with a chance to form a government.
Luxon told supporters gathered in Auckland that while it looked like his party had a pathway to form the next government, the race remained “too close to call.”
He said the country would need to wait until the Electoral Commission delivered the final official results on November 27 for certainty. Coalition negotiations could then drag on for weeks before a government is formed.
The first-term government’s struggle to secure an emphatic victory signifies the level of public discontent over high gas prices and other living costs, stubbornly high unemployment rates and healthcare.
In an unusual dynamic, swing voters abandoned the traditionally dominant players –  center-right National and the center-left Labour party – opting instead to support minor parties across the political spectrum.
Preliminary numbers show the right-wing coalition grouping has 67 seats in an expanded 131-seat parliament, but nearly 400,000 votes cast under special circumstances – including those of New Zealanders who live overseas – have yet to be counted.
Should the coalition eventually fall short of a majority, Luxon would likely need to turn to the progressive centrist Opportunity party for support.
The party,  which positions itself as both business-and climate-friendly, made history on Saturday, projected to become the first total outsider party to enter the country’s parliament in three decades.
Prior to the election, Luxon had ruled out working with the party led by millennial political newcomer Qiulae Wong. But he stuck a more conciliatory tone on Sunday morning.
“I actually do want to build a relationship with her as the leader and also with her party, and try and find common ground,” he said, congratulating the party for its achievement.
The opposition grouping of Labour, the leftist Greens and indigenous party Te Pati Māori is projected to have 57 seats. But the bloc could have a path to power if it picked up some additional seats in the final count, and if it secured the support of Opportunity.
Labour Leader Chris Hipkins made light of Saturday’s inconclusive results as he addressed supporters in Wellington, saying: “Tonight, New Zealand has spoken. It may take us a little bit longer to figure out exactly what it is that you’ve said.”
Hipkins, who served briefly as prime minister in 2023, did not concede, telling the crowd that “every vote matters. And every vote must be counted.”
Labour received the highest share of the popular vote under the country’s mixed-member proportional voting system by a tiny margin, but a stronger performance in individual electorates has delivered National more seats in parliament.
The National-led coalition – the country’s most right-wing in a generation – took power in 2023, capitalizing on an electorate looking for change in the wake of the Covid-19 pandemic.
Its ability to deliver on a pledge to get the country “back on track” economically has been hamstrung by the global uncertainty created by US President Donald Trump’s tariff offensive and the soaring fuel prices that have resulted from the US-Israeli war with Iran.
Luxon urged voters to “stick with the plan.” But his party emerges a diminished force, crashing to just 29.2% of the popular vote, down from 38.1% in 2023, according to the preliminary count.
Its coalition partners, the right-wing-libertarian ACT party and the nationalist New Zealand First Party, increased their vote share to 10.9% and 9.8% respectively, putting them both in a stronger position to dictate terms in pending coalition talks.
The stronger-than-expected result for New Zealand First and ACT, and National’s weakened position, raises the prospect of the coalition moving further to the right in a second term and further embracing culture-war policies.
On the campaign trail the ACT vowed to end affirmative action schemes at the country’s medical schools, while New Zealand First promised sweeping immigration changes and voiced support for a review of the ban on gay conversion therapy.
Luxon, would also have a complex job filling key cabinet posts in a second term, with a raft of senior lawmakers from his National party, including finance minister Nicola Willis and parliament’s speaker Gerry Brownlee, losing their seats.
The two parties that have dominated Wellington politics for nearly a century fell out of favor with swing voters, with National and Labour each attracting just 29% of the popular vote. Those votes instead went to minor parties entrenched further to the right and the left, as well as Opportunity in the center.
Wong, 38, a former sustainable business consultant who applied for the party’s leadership by responding to a job advertisement a year ago , told supporters they had voted “to change New Zealand politics for good.”
The party, which secured nearly 6% of the vote, becomes the first party not involving established political figures to win enough support to enter parliament since the country moved to a mixed-member proportional voting system in the mid-1990s.
Depending on the final vote tally, Opportunity could still find itself in the kingmaker position – with both the right and the left groupings vying for its support.

articles.title_orig: With an ode to mate tea, pope urges faithful in Uruguay to build bridges of fraternity and faith
articles.title_zh: With an ode to mate tea, pope urges faithful in Uruguay to build bridges of fraternity and faith
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV waves after meeting with Uruguay's President Yamandu Orsi at Plaza Independencia in Montevideo, Uruguay, Friday, Nov. 6, 2026. Matilde Campodonico /AP hide caption
MONTEVIDEO, Uruguay — Pope Leo XIV has arrived in South America for a 12-day, three-country journey that will be his longest and most far-reaching trip yet, and his first major overseas visit since undergoing lung cancer surgery.
Along the way Leo will take 12 flights, including two helicopter rides, give 36 speeches and visit 10 cities including Cusco, Peru, which sits more than 11,000 feet above sea level. Even the heartiest of travelers can experience altitude sickness there and may require supplemental oxygen.
Last month, Leo underwent surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung. Vatican officials say he has completed his two-week recovery period and requires no further treatment.
The Vatican's new communications chief Maria Montserrat Alvarado said the pontiff was eager to begin his journey. "His doctors are very confident and he'll have plenty of medical care on board should something happen," she said.
A proposed papal address to the parliament triggered a swift rebuke from the public and politicians alike and was quickly scrapped. Instead, Uruguay's left-wing President Yamandú Orsi presided over the welcome ceremony outside Montevideo's main cathedral.
Crowds of up to 30,000 people, according to the Vatican, had lined the streets to catch a glimpse of Pope Leo as he drove past in his Popemobile.
But the crowd gathered to greet him at the central Plaza Independencia was much smaller, not even filling half the length of the vast square. Those who came were nonetheless delighted to see him and hear his message.
Pope Leo XIV is transported to the Cathedral in Montevideo, Uruguay, Friday, Nov. 6, 2026. Natacha Pisarenko/AP hide caption
The Pope wasted little time addressing Uruguay's secular traditions and its liberal laws on abortion and euthanasia. Uruguay was the first country in Latin America to legalize euthanasia through legislation, and, in 2012, became the second in the region to legalize abortion, after Cuba.
Speaking in Spanish, Leo emphasized the importance of protecting family life and delivered a pointed criticism of both laws.
He said: "It is everyone's responsibility to ensure that each person can live with dignity, receive the care they need, and be accompanied until the natural end of his or her life."
It's a puzzling choice for the first leg of the pope's anticipated return to South America, where he spent two decades in Peru, first as a missionary then as Bishop of the coastal city of Chiclayo. Uruguay, a small nation of around 3.5 million people, where adoring crowds will be small, is famously Latin America's most secular nation.
When asked why go to Uruguay at all, given the high rate of atheists and strict separation of church and state, communications chief Alvarado answered simply, "Why Not?" Adding, "the Gospel is meant to go everywhere."
Few welcome banners are seen throughout the capital Montevideo, except for large posters of a waving Pope Leo adorning city churches. A huge banner drapes down the facade of the Blessed Sacrament Church, in Montevideo's upscale Pocitos neighborhood, where 70-year old retiree Ana Maria Saprissa was heading for quiet prayer.
We are thankful, agradecida , she says that the pontiff is coming to visit. "His visit gives us such joy because … he remembered us all here in this tiny country that has so many needs," she says.
Uruguay's tradition of separating religion from government and public life dates back more than a century. Christmas has long been officially referred to as Family Day, while Easter week is given the vacation-friendly name Tourism Week.
Only about a third of Uruguayans identify as Catholics and even less say they practice the religion, according to political analyst Mariana Pomiés , director of the public polling firm CIFRA.
Children attend Pope Leo XIV's meeting with government officials, civil society representatives and diplomats at Plaza Independencia in Montevideo, on the first day of his 12-day apostolic journey to South America, Friday, Nov. 6, 2026. Andrew Medichini/AP hide caption
But as a practicing Catholic, Pomiés says sometimes Uruguayan and especially officials misinterpret what secularism is. "Secularism is not anti-religion, it's the neutrality of the state in religious matters. But here the neutrality se convirtió en un absoluto … it became an absolute."
Dozens of volunteers cleaned streets, mowed lawns and erected a simple stage outside the tiny brick Our Lady of Guadalupe Church. It's the focal spot for many in the Casavalle neighbourhood, a working-class area about a half hour north of Montevideo, where the pope is scheduled to visit on Saturday.
"I am very happy, very glad, very grateful … that eyes have been set here," where many are forgotten and stigmatised, said Father Pablo Coimbra, who's served as the community's pastoral leader for the past six years.
On Sunday, he heads to Florida, a town about an hour outside the capital, for an open-air Mass at the National Shrine of Our Lady of the Thirty-Three — a figure closely associated with Uruguay's struggle for independence from Brazilian rule in 1825.
By Sunday evening, Pope Leo will be in neighboring Argentina, arriving in Buenos Aires on a visit that fulfils a wish of his predecessor, Pope Francis, who had hoped to return to his homeland but never made the journey.
Before his death, Francis had said he didn't want a papal visit to become entangled in Argentina's intensely polarized politics.
Pope Leo's visit to Argentina offers an early test of how he will address the Catholic Church's differences with right-wing populist leaders gaining ground across Latin America. Those tensions have also surfaced in the U.S., where Leo has clashed with President Trump over immigration and the treatment of migrants.
Far-right President Javier Milei's sweeping austerity measures, which have pushed millions of Argentines into poverty, could put him at odds with Leo, who has long championed the poor.
Milei has also embraced data centers and a largely unfettered approach to artificial intelligence regulation, while Pope Leo's inaugural encyclical called for ethical caution and safeguards to protect human dignity in the age of AI.
The upper section of a statue of Pope Leo XIV is transported to 'El Niño' park in Callao, Lima, Peru, Friday, Nov. 6, 2026, where it will be installed ahead of his planned trip to Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru from Nov. 6 to17. Guadalupe Pardo/AP hide caption
The final stop is Peru, where Leo's visit is being billed as a homecoming.
As a missionary priest and later Bishop of the coastal city of Chiclayo, Pope Leo spent two decades in the country. He became a naturalized Peruvian in 2015, and has said the country shaped his life more than anything else.
He will visit several cities and towns where he lived and will meet with President Keiko Fujimori , the daughter of former Peruvian dictator Alberto Fujimori.
As a priest during the Fujimori dictatorship, Leo was openly critical of military violence and human rights abuses and supported efforts leading to Peru's Truth and Reconciliation Commission following the return to democracy.
But for many Uruguayans Pope Leo is not very well known. Walking past the huge stage set up for Leo's welcoming ceremony, Juan Martin Guerreiro said he wasn't sure he would attend the pope's speeches.
"He doesn't feel as influential to me … as Pope Francis," said Guerreiro. But he said he's willing to give the new pope a chance because he is South American.
When reminded that Pope Leo was born in Chicago, Guerreiro said he wouldn't hold that against him.

articles.title_orig: Germans wrestle with what to do with Hitler's destroyed Eagle's Nest retreat
articles.title_zh: Germans wrestle with what to do with Hitler's destroyed Eagle's Nest retreat
articles.content_orig:
Perched on a ridge high up in the spectacular scenery of the German Alps lie the burned-out ruins of a mountain house called The Eagle's Nest, which is now at the heart of an intense debate about Germany's Nazi past.
Known in German as Kehlsteinhaus, the retreat was built by the Nazis in 1938, and frequented by Adolf Hitler and other high-ranking Nazis and their guests. After World War Two it was classified as a historical monument recalling the Nazi era.
Last month it was gutted by fire in a suspected arson attack, and some believe it should be completely destroyed, the site returned to nature and all memory of its Nazi past forgotten.
But others want it either partially or completely rebuilt, wary of the risk of turning it into a site for Neo-Nazi pilgrimage at a time when Germany is witnessing the resurgence of the far-right.
Germany has an "everlasting responsibility to communicate, to deal with our Nazi past", said Isabel Heinemann, professor of contemporary history at Munich's Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität (LMU).
But rebuilding the site completely, she warned, would mean putting "highly ideologised or highly ideological architecture" back in place.
Before it was burned down during the evening of 23 October, the Eagle's Nest had been a popular tourist attraction, owned by the state of Bavaria and operating for many years as a restaurant.
Visitors would take a bus and then ride the original brass and mirror-panelled lift through the mountain to the Kehlsteinhaus to savour the magnificent views above the town of Berchtesgaden.
Once there, they could eat sausages in the beer garden on the Obersalzberg at 1,834m (6,017ft) above sea level, overlooking the Alps.
Unlike Hitler's nearby summer residence, the Berghof, which was bombed in World War Two and demolished in 1952, the Eagle's Nest survived the war.
Tens of thousands of tourists visited each season, providing an important source of income to the region.
In the 1990s, amid concerns that the site did not do enough to confront the crimes of the Nazi past, a museum, the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, was opened close by.
Around 15 years ago, a photo exhibit was opened in the Kehlsteinhaus about its history.
Although the Eagle's Nest itself was "largely destroyed" by the fire, according to police, the documentation centre survived unscathed.
The authorities have not commented on a possible motive, but a 33-year-old man with a history of mental illness has been detained in a secure psychiatric hospital on suspicion of arson.
Some feel this is the moment to allow the site to fade into history.
"It's been torched now. It's been destroyed. I think they should just clear away the rubble and leave the mountain as it should be in its natural state," said Prof Sir Richard J. Evans, a specialist in Nazi Germany at the University of Cambridge.
That has happened with "quite a few other Nazi sites", he argued, including the bunker in Berlin where Hitler killed himself: "The bunker was filled in with concrete and a children's playground put on the top of it on the ground."
The Kehlsteinhaus was just "a Nazi vanity project" since romanticised by the name Eagle's Nest, he said.
But Bavaria's authorities take a different view about the site's future.
Both the state's interior minister, Joachim Herrmann, and its minister for the arts, Markus Blume, have spoken out in favour of rebuilding the Kehlsteinhaus.
"We can hardly leave a ruin standing there," Herrmann said.
Sven Keller, head of the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, believes it is important not to leave the site in ruins, as that could encourage Neo-Nazi pilgrims, who would be able to hike up there completely undisturbed.
"We have quite some experience at Obersalzberg with what happens if we clear those sites. Hitler's Berghof was demolished in the 1950s, and in our experience, this does not remove such sites from the mental maps of people," he told the BBC's Today programme.
Nor does he believe "a one-on-one reconstruction" of the site is possible, and Blume has made clear on Bavarian radio that "it should not and must not cost the taxpayer anything".
Herrmann said they would look for a sensible solution in consultation with historians, given the historically complex circumstances surrounding the building.
Heinemann, who also heads the Leibniz Institute for Contemporary History, believes full-scale reconstruction should be "out of the question".
"I rather think we can document the state left by the fire and also document the historical remains of the Kehlsteinhaus, and then reconstruct parts in a modern design, to make clear the different layers of time that can be seen in this building," she told the BBC.
Germany and Austria have long struggled to deal with the fraught legacy of buildings and sites connected to the Nazi era.
With the recent rise of the far-right AfD and the Austrian Freedom Party, the debate over Erinnerungskultur (Culture of Remembrance) has taken on a new urgency.
A row broke out recently in Germany when AfD and conservative CDU councillors in a town in Saxony decided to ban "stumbling stones" memorials - embedded small brass plaques in the streets - to victims of the Nazis.
In Austria over the summer, a police station was opened in the house where Hitler was born in Braunau am Inn. It followed years of controversy about how the house should be used.
The Austrian government said the police presence would help prevent neo-Nazi pilgrims.
But others had wanted the house to become a centre of responsibility, actively confronting the Nazi past.
As one resident of Braunau am Inn told me, it was a delicate balance between how much to remember and how much to forget.

articles.title_orig: Ocarina of Time review: Does Nintendo's Zelda remake match its original?
articles.title_zh: Ocarina of Time review: Does Nintendo's Zelda remake match its original?
articles.content_orig:
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time was finally released on Thursday, after years of rumours that Nintendo would remake the game - considered one of the best ever made.
IGN called it "the biggest game of the decade" in their review when it launched in 1998 on the N64, and it set the standard for 3D games.
A lot of the things we take for granted in modern games - such as riding a horse, fighting with a sword and shield, or locking on to enemies with the tap of a button - were pioneered or perfected in Ocarina of Time.
It received an almost perfect score from critics and, decades on, remains the highest-rated game in history on Metacritic, which aggregates reviews.
So how do you remake what many consider a masterpiece?
Those like me who grew up playing the original will feel right at home here.
Nintendo has decided against reinventing the wheel, instead producing something which plays very similarly to the N64 classic.
As I've said before , video game remakes are a bit different to film or TV - gaming fans often clamour for a new take on their favourites, hoping developers harness evolution in tech to make them fresh.
And games have come a long way in the almost 30 years since the original Ocarina of Time came out.
"When you compare the games in the past and the games in modern times, so to speak, the norms of what people expect from a game have evolved naturally," Nintendo producer Hidemaro Fujibayashi told me.
"In the past, games where the users may have needed more imagination to fill the blanks or the gaps are now clearly expressed through the graphics that they see on the screen."
But fancy graphics have come at a price - a pivot away from realism into something a bit more cartoonish. Some might even be disappointed by this, given the N64 game had quite horrifying elements in places.
One was the Skulltula House, a room where people had been morphed into human-spider hybrids.
"Back when we created the original Ocarina of Time, the means to convey or express ideas was limited compared with what we have now," series producer Eiji Aonuma - who worked on the original game - said.
"With regard to even the so-called scary elements, we strove to add a touch of the comical."
But he told the BBC that enhanced graphics and lighting capabilities unintentionally exaggerated the already-spooky Skulltula House and its potential to strike fear into players.
"When we carried out the test play, the testers were telling us, 'Oh, this is too scary'," he said. "So of course, in the end product, we've made the necessary adjustments so that we can retain the same balance that we had achieved in the original."
I spoke to a few YouTubers about the upcoming game to get their thoughts - and the response was overwhelmingly positive.
Mike Channell, co-editor of the YouTube channel Outside Xbox, said he believed the remake had been made "very meticulously" in the hopes of living up to fan expectations.
"Having played the game, it's clear that serious thought has gone into every decision, to the point where I'm not convinced this remake has taken any less time and effort than an all-new Zelda game," he said.
"Ocarina of Time is obviously one of the great video game experiences in the history of the medium, but I have no doubt this new version will be the best way to experience this story.
"It's fleshed out as a world, sumptuously detailed, and the controls match 21st-Century expectations."
Ed King, known as Zeltik to his 893,000 followers on YouTube, said "the level of detail and charm" in the Ocarina of Time remake stood out.
"The Forest Temple has always been my favourite Zelda dungeon: a mysterious, haunted mansion in the deep woods, a lost work of man slowly being reclaimed by nature," he said. "The remake really leans into the surreal, uncanny nature of the original dungeon."
And fellow YouTuber StrawHatMidas said it was the "perfect" way to "bring this classic back".
"Not only does the game pay homage to the Nintendo 64 original, but it also expands on the things that made it so memorable," he said. "Everything from the world and atmosphere to the controls and soundtrack feels like a love letter to the classic Zelda formula."
Nintendo has made some big changes, not least to the Water Temple - a dungeon about two thirds into the game.
Aonuma said, having worked on the original, this was what he personally wanted to change most due to its reputation for being "very, very difficult".
He said there was now "a greater facility in tackling" the dungeon, as players can now easily change a critical in-game item known as heavy boots and have "the ability to leverage the camera orientation".
I grew up playing Zelda on the N64, which pioneered the joystick - but nowadays two sticks is the standard, with one to move and one to control the camera.
As far as I'm concerned, being able to freely move the camera this time round was a significant improvement.
At times, the trip down memory lane was captivating. I knew where to go and what to do, thanks to a kind of muscle memory. However, on occasion that took away from the experience - with some tasks achieved too easily and some puzzles too quickly because I recalled their solutions.
Some people will love how similar it is, but I have to wonder if Nintendo has played things a bit too safe.
I don't think the developers see it that way.
"Even if the game may look different, we've maintained the essence that the original developers wanted to and hopefully conveyed through the original Ocarina of Time," Fujibayashi said.
Don't get me wrong - the game has lots of changes and surprises, and I won't spoil them, but I wish there had been more.
Then again, perhaps the best games leave you wanting more.
Or as Mike put it: "I loved the original as much as the next person, but I don't think I'll be going back to it."
Fans will no doubt wonder whether this is it, or if there will be more Zelda on the horizon. With the franchise's first movie coming next year, there's certainly more to come in the short term.
And in the long term, I wondered if with 30 more years of technological advancements, Nintendo might consider remaking the game once again.
"I will be long retired," Aonuma said, with a laugh.

articles.title_orig: Drone and missile attacks wound 9 in Ukraine as country prepares for talks with Russia and US
articles.title_zh: Drone and missile attacks wound 9 in Ukraine as country prepares for talks with Russia and US
articles.content_orig:
Moscow used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in attacks on electricity substations and bridge over the Dnipro
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia of trying to “plunge Kyiv and the entire country into a blackout”, after a major attack overnight on energy infrastructure in the capital and a bridge over the Dnipro River.
Ukraine’s president said Moscow’s preparations for peace talks next week involved pummelling a city of millions with ballistic missiles.
Negotiators from Russia , Ukraine and the US are due to meet on Tuesday and Wednesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at ending the war.
Zelenskyy appealed to the US Congress – won by the Democrats in the midterm elections – to pay more attention to Ukraine in the face of relentless Russian bombardment. “Ukraine must not be left alone. We are counting on increased bilateral support from the US,” he said .
Russia used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in its latest attack on Kyiv and surrounding regions. The city faced serious difficulties with its electricity, water and heat supplies, Zelenskyy said, with five people injured including a 14-year-old girl.
The strikes targeted substations in five regions, including one connecting two nuclear power plants to Kyiv. The city’s Northern Bridge, a key transport artery, was closed on Saturday as workers repaired damage to the road’s surface and power lines.
The attacks cap a dire week for residents in Kyiv, who have experienced day-long power cuts and interruptions to the water supply. Ukrainian officials say the Kremlin’s goal is to freeze civilians into submission over the brutal winter months, a war crime.
They have little confidence that US-backed peace talks will yield concrete results. In an interview with CNN , Zelenskyy described the latest blueprint set out by Jared Kushner, Donald Trump’s son-in-law, as “Yalta 2.0” – a reference to the 1945 summit between Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill that divided postwar Europe.
In a series of social media posts , Kushner said the discussions would include a new security framework for Europe, alongside guarantees for Ukraine. This appears to be a reference to the Kremlin’s longstanding demand that Nato’s expansion across Europe be reversed.
after newsletter promotion
Speaking on Friday, Trump said a “big beautiful agreement” could be close, involving “all of Europe”. Shortly before invading Ukraine, the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, demanded that Nato go back to its pre-1997 posture – before the Baltic states and nations in eastern Europe and the Balkans joined.
Ukraine and its European partners are deeply sceptical. “The idea of discussing European-Russian security infrastructure is not simple, and it can be dangerous,” Zelenskyy told CNN, emphasising: “We don’t want to be divided by Russia.”
Zelenskyy said Moscow had to end its war first, with Ukraine given meaningful security guarantees. After that, “depending on the answers”, wider security architecture could be considered, he said. Western diplomats say agreeing to Russia’s demands would effectively end Nato.
Russia’s defence ministry, meanwhile, said its strikes early on Saturday were against energy and transport targets. Since the summer, it has dramatically stepped up air attacks on Ukrainian cities, as its progress on the frontline has stalled. Last month Russia lost 54,000 troops, killed or injured, according to Kyiv – the highest monthly loss in the war.

When Ford gave its iconic Mustang a dramatic redesign for the 2015 model year, the car came with a lot of big changes. One came out back, where the Mustang moved to a standard independent rear suspension for the first time in its existence. Another big change came under the hood, where Ford added the turbocharged 2.3-liter EcoBoost engine as the Mustang's volume engine option. A couple years later, with the old V6 dropped from the lineup, the EcoBoost four-cylinder became — and still is — the Mustang's base engine.
However, despite being the base engine, and despite upsetting some Mustang purists with its lack of displacement, it's hard to argue the Mustang's 2.3 EcoBoost is lacking in the horsepower department. The base model 2026 Mustang EcoBoost is rated at 315 horsepower, which is in fact, the same horsepower rating as the 2010 V8-powered Mustang GT, with the EcoBoost also outpowering previous V8 Mustang GTs of the '90s and 2000s as well.
The latest Ford Mustang EcoBoost is a car that shows just how far four-cylinder performance has come, but on the modern enthusiast market, it's not even the most powerful four-cylinder option.. To demonstrate this, we've rounded up five different four-cylinder vehicles that outgun the Mustang in horsepower rating, with a mix of cars that includes everything from hot hatchbacks to sport sedans, and even a crossover SUV.
Back in the '90s and '2000s, high-performance Honda and Acura vehicles were known for their unique, high-revving naturally aspirated engines. Today, though, Honda has fully embraced turbocharging, and the powerful Honda Civic Type R is known as one of the fastest front-wheel-drive cars in the world. In terms of horsepower ratings, the 2.0-liter turbocharged four-cylinder powering the latest Civic Type R ties the Mustang EcoBoost with the same 315-horsepower rating, but Honda builds another hot hatchback that actually edges both of them out in the power department.
That car is the highly enjoyable Acura Integra Type S, which is a closely related and slightly more upmarket sibling to the Civic Type R, using the same platform and the same 2.0-liter turbo engine. While the Acura and Honda engines are basically identical, the Integra uses a more aggressive exhaust system, which boosts its output by five horsepower, for a total of 320.
Head-to-head comparisons between the two Honda products show that the Integra's isn't enough to give the heavier Acura an edge in performance, but both cars are still considered among the best hot hatchbacks you can buy. Notably, the Integra Type S is very well matched against the Mustang EcoBoost in performance metrics, leaving buyers to choose between the Acura's precision and practicality or the Ford's rear-drive personality.
With American automakers being world-famous for their V8 engines, you'd expect most of the Mustang EcoBoost's top four-cylinder rivals to come from German or Japanese brands, and that's the case for most of the picks in this selection. However, Ford's arch-rival, General Motors, also has a very potent, four-cylinder engine of its own — and both larger and more powerful than the Ford 2.3. That engine is GM's 2.7-liter turbocharged four-cylinder, which is known as the L3B.
The 2.7 turbo is primarily found in Chevrolet and GMC pickup trucks, where its 310-horsepower rating comes in just below the Mustang EcoBoost's output. However, in the high-performance Cadillac CT4-V sport sedan , the L3B gets a few tweaks that push its peak output to 325 horsepower. The four-cylinder-powered CT4-V isn't on the the same level as the flagship CT4-V Blackwing with its twin-turbo V6, but the regular CT4-V is still very quick, capable of hitting 60 miles per hour in less than five seconds.
With the Cadillac CT4 being discontinued at the end of the 2026 model year, GM will have to hand the four-cylinder horsepower crown back to Ford, at least for the time being. Speculation suggests that GM is hard at work on a new lineup of rear-drive models, potentially including a reborn version of the Mustang's longtime rival, the Chevrolet Camaro. If and when those new GM models arrive, we wouldn't be surprised to see a turbo four-cylinder engine option that's at least equal to the current L3B.
Viewed as a whole, today's market doesn't have nearly the same number of affordably priced performance cars that we saw in decades past — but at least the hot hatchback segment is alive and well, with several great choices for enthusiasts. One of these choices is the Volkswagen Golf R, which pushes Volkswagen's four-cylinder performance to a new level.
Sharing its DNA with the iconic Golf GTI, the Golf R elevates the GTI's performance in a big way, adding an all-wheel-drive system and giving Volkswagen's turbocharged 2.0-liter four-cylinder engine a major bump in power. Already quick to start, Volkswagen updated the Golf R for the 2025 model year, which boosted its output to a stout 328 horsepower. With that aforementioned 4Motion AWD system, this well-appointed Volkswagen can rocket to 60 miles per hour in the low four-second range, making the Golf R one of the quickest and most mature hatchbacks you can buy .
Additionally, if we are going to talk about the Golf R, we also have to mention its closely related corporate cousin, the Audi S3. The S3 essentially puts the Golf R's powertrain into a sedan, and has the same 328-horsepower rating as its Volkswagen counterpart. With these German offerings, buyers can choose their preferred brand and body style, but in either case they'll be getting one of the most potent four-cylinder engines on the market today.
With the legendary reputation of the Porsche 911 and its flat-six engine, some car enthusiasts might not associate Porsche with high-powered four-cylinder engines, but Porsche has made a good few of those as well. The company has a long history of building impressive four-piston motors, and the engine from the Porsche 718 Cayman S and its Boxster S sibling is among the most powerful road-going examples around.
Displacing 2.5 liters, the flat-four engine that powers the 718 Cayman and Boxster S is rated at an even 350 horsepower. When the car debuted in 2017, during Car & Driver's testing, the Cayman S hit 60 miles per hour in just 3.6 seconds. What's also unique about the 718's four-cylinder engines is that, unlike the Mustang's EcoBoost 2.3 and the other inline-four engines on this list, the Porsche flat-four design is unique specifically to the Cayman and Boxsters, and not shared with other mainstream models.
Sure, some Porsche fans might recommend that you skip the four-cylinder models and go straight for the wonderful, flat-six-powered Cayman GTS or GT4, and there are lots of reasons one might want to do that. However, both when viewed on its own merits and when compared to other four-cylinder engines on the market, the Porsche 2.5 is easily among the best out there.
Given their relatively small displacement, it's no surprise that the engines on this list — including the Ford 2.3 EcoBoost itself — all use turbocharging to hit their impressive power levels. Toyota, though, has a potent 2.5-liter four-cylinder-powered vehicle that beats the Mustang's output without using a turbocharger.
Instead, the powertrain in the 2026 Toyota RAV4 Plug-In Hybrid uses a combination of an internal combustion four-cylinder engine and three electric motors to make a combined total of 324 horsepower. The result is one of the quickest mainstream compact crossover SUVs you can buy, capable of hitting 60 miles per hour in the low five-second range.
Sure, the RAV4 PHEV's high curb weight and family crossover DNA might keep it from ever being a serious performance machine in the way other cars on this list might be, but the unexpected nature of its horsepower is part of the fun. This redesign takes advantage of the existing background layer that’s currently just home to the logo/wordmark, search, and account menu.

Hate the idea of just the pinned "bobble head" look. I like being able to view message tidbits.  Plus, it's directly copying Apple (enough said). I have to use an iPhone at my job. I hate the pinned bubble conversation look and more importantly it's function.
Otherwise, you’ll see a circular magnifying glass icon and “Start chat” in the pill. The animation that accompanies this change looks nice and feels alive, while boosting one-handed usability.
Google has replaced the Gemini FAB with a button in the top-right corner next to your profile image. This matches the design leveraged by Workspace apps on desktop and mobile.
These updates are currently in the beta channel and not yet widely rolled out to all testers. Some users have all aspects of the redesign, but it appears that Google is rolling out the various components in a piecemeal fashion.

articles.title_orig: King Charles would ‘carefully’ consider China visit
articles.title_zh: King Charles would ‘carefully’ consider China visit
articles.content_orig:
By REBECCA ENGLISH, ROYAL EDITOR and GLEN OWEN
Published: 18:29 EDT, 7 November 2026 | Updated: 18:59 EDT, 7 November 2026
King Charles would be prepared to undertake a controversial state visit to China if requested by Prime Minister Andy Burnham , sources indicated on Saturday.
As Charles is recovering from his 'challenging' Caribbean tour dominated by rows over slavery reparations, Buckingham Palace was not ruling out an even more politically testing trip to Beijing .
Such a visit would be the first by a British monarch to the communist country for 40 years, but would be fraught with controversy given the ongoing security threat posed by China to Britain. One Whitehall source told The Mail on Sunday: 'We understand the King would be quite up for it, if it came to it.'
But a senior Tory source said: 'This would be seen as seriously divisive politics.'
Royal insiders stress a trip isn't on the table yet and would come with 'complex' logistical and political issues to navigate.
As Prince of Wales, Charles made no secret of his antipathy to the Chinese regime. But a royal aide said: 'If the government said 'Will the King go to China?' I think we would think about it very carefully.
'China is a hugely important country... a very complex country. It would pose a lot of complexity in putting a programme together. This is the 40th anniversary of the last state visit.'
It comes amid a battle within the Government over whether to confront or appease Beijing. Security officials have complained that Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband is leading the 'appease' camp as the UK is so reliant on China for the supply of solar panels central to his Net Zero climate agenda.
King Charles III during his tour of Antigua and Barbuda. The Palace has not ruled the King travelling on a politically testing trip to Beijing
Prime Minister Andy Burnham. A battle is raging within the Government over whether to confront or appease Beijing
As heir to the throne, Charles maintained a highly–critical stance over the Chinese government, particularly as a result of his support for Tibet and the Dalai Lama. He boycotted UK state banquets for presidents Jiang Zemin in 1999 and Hu Jintao in 2005 over China's human rights record.
He once described Chinese officials as 'appalling old waxworks', and also wriggled out of a state banquet to honour president Xi Jinping in 2015.
Despite mounting evidence of state–sponsored activities in the UK, such as cyber attacks and political infiltration, Mr Miliband supports closer ties with China. One of his first moves as Foreign Secretary was to arrange to meet Chinese foreign minister Wang Yi.
Former Tory leader Iain Duncan Smith said: 'If it is true the King might be going to China it is utterly appalling. They are effectively at war with us, and should not be rewarded for it.'
Diplomats believe the King's Caribbean tour was a success, particularly his visit to Guyana, where he was welcomed with open arms at a time when China is making huge inroads in the region.
If rumours are correct, the King is to be wheeled out as Britain's version of 'panda diplomacy' and sent to Communist China.
Is this a state visit too far? I think it is. The issue is not Charles. He has shown himself a master of sensitive visits, whether to the US under erratic Donald Trump or to the Caribbean, where slavery reparations dominated discussion.
No, the question is: why are we debasing ourselves by offering a visit to a China leadership that behaves so destructively towards us? It would be ironic. The debate about historic slavery in the Caribbean pales against China's record of using forced labour now in its cotton and potentially other industries, including silicon used in solar panels that Net Zero fanatic Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband wants to cover the British countryside with. And we reward this with a state visit?
Too often our leaders, especially on the Left, continue the delusion that China is an economic El Dorado which will make us rich. But Beijing does not want free trade. It wants to make others dependent on it. This is not trade as a tool of joint prosperity but trade as a weapon in conflict.
Rather than organising a cringeworthy visit, our leaders' time would be better spent standing up for our values and interests and articulating them clearly.

articles.title_zh: Binance’s CFO Is Out a Week After $6.3 Billion Hack
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Hackers took about $6.3 billion from Binance last week. Michael Saylor now warns that attackers armed with artificial intelligence (AI) will hunt the weakest software holding customer money.
That risk sits with anyone who keeps coins on an exchange. Binance says it has refilled most of the stolen funds from its reserves, yet the breach began with an old trick, a fake job interview.
Saylor chairs MicroStrategy, a company whose main asset is Bitcoin (BTC). At the OranjeBTC Summit in São Paulo, he was asked about Binance and a second breach in Brazil.
On November 2, security firm Hypernative flagged more than $40 million in suspicious transfers from Mercado Bitcoin, a Brazilian exchange.
Saylor said frontier AI models, the most advanced systems from labs like Anthropic and OpenAI, make hackers far more capable.
"The real threat is someone, a very focused AI hacker, aimed at new software not properly tested, not locked down, that someone rushed into production too quickly."
He urged exchanges, banks and custodians to run those models daily against their own systems.
"Bitcoin's sound. Rickety, poorly constructed digital commerce software is going to be hacked."
He added that every new feature on Ethereum, Solana or Cardano gives attackers another way in.
Binance says a fake recruiter got an engineer to download a fake job "assignment."
Attackers then used Binance's own internal AI tool to take over other staff accounts. Still, the attack relied mainly on ordinary phishing, Fortune said.
The FBI blamed North Korea. TRM Labs tied it to TraderTraitor, the unit the FBI blamed for the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in 2025.
Tether and Circle froze stolen stablecoins, tokens pegged to the US dollar.
Binance now plans to expand AI-powered threat detection. Meanwhile, India's cyber agency warned on November 4 of an AI-assisted hacker group stealing wallet keys from crypto exchanges.
The next test is Binance's updated proof of reserves, a public check that it still holds customers' coins, due once repairs finish.
